Lesson 7 · Evaluate the action

Do replenishment alerts actually help?

The forecast identifies stores that may struggle. The director now needs evidence that a replenishment alert changes the outcome enough to justify paying for it.

Randomized pilot · S001–S050 · weeks 17–24

Method in this decision: Randomized evaluation

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The decision brief

The chain runs a pilot in 50 stores. It randomly assigns 25 to receive enabled alerts and a standard weekly replenishment review; 25 continue usual operations. The outcome is each store’s average stockout rate over weeks 17–24. The business decision combines the reduction in unavailable products with the cost of delivering the service. This is the first intervention study in the course.

Define exactly what “help” means

Name the intervention, unit, and outcome

  • Unit: a store eligible for the pilot.
  • Treatment: an offer of replenishment alerts beginning in week 17.
  • Outcome: the store’s average stockout rate in weeks 17–24.
  • Contrast: usual operations versus the alert offer.

Predicting that a store will struggle is different from predicting how an alert changes its outcome. A causal question compares alternative interventions for the same unit at the same time. Define the offer precisely enough that another team could implement it.

Every store has two potential policy outcomes

Y(0): usual-operation rate; Y(1): alert-offer rate; reduction = Y(0) − Y(1)

We use a positive reduction to mean improvement. A store reveals only the outcome under the policy it actually receives. The missing alternative is the counterfactual. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference: observing more detail about the factual outcome does not reveal the same store’s other policy path.

Different averages answer different spending questions

Choose the target before calculating an effect
TargetWhose reductions are averaged?
ATEAll stores in the named target population
ATTStores that receive the offer
ATUStores that do not receive it

ATE = treated share × ATT + untreated share × ATU

Effects can vary across delivery times and locations, so these averages need not coincide. In this teaching world alerts reduce stockouts by different amounts across store types. In other businesses an intervention could also help some units and harm others; define the average without assuming identical responses.

Observed outcomes follow assignment

Observed Y = (1 − D)Y(0) + DY(1), where D is the offer indicator

The observed usual-minus-offer group difference is directly calculable. In an observational comparison, it combines the treated group’s causal reduction with a baseline difference between the groups. Random assignment removes systematic selection in expectation, allowing the comparison to estimate the pilot population’s average effect.

Define the action and the unit of assignment

An alert is a weekly list of low-stock products sent before the replenishment review. The store team reviews that list and brings forward orders when appropriate. In this exercise, every offered store receives the service as assigned. The comparison group continues its existing process during the same eight weeks.

The randomization unit is the store. Aggregate its eight outcomes into one post-period average before comparing groups. This keeps the analysis aligned with the 50 independently assigned stores, rather than treating 400 weekly rows as 400 separate assignments.

The accounting scenario charges 6 CU for each stockout product-day. Alerts add 12 CU per store-week in service fees and 8 CU in extra inventory holding cost. This cost rule is a stated management input, not an estimate of lost sales.

Make the experiment interpretable before it starts

Randomization is a procedure, not a table appearance

Pilot baseline balance
Starting characteristicOffered storesUsual-operation stores
lead_days3.603.88
urban0.600.48
baseline_rate12.8612.96

Record the eligibility list, random assignment, offer date, and exposure. Chance imbalances can remain in a particular draw; perfect equality is not required. Assignment records are stronger evidence of randomization than a collection of nonsignificant balance tests.

Keep the intervention and comparison stable

  • Define one operational version of the alert offer.
  • Track whether the offer is delivered and used.
  • Avoid spillovers between the assigned store groups.
  • Measure the same outcome and follow-up window in both groups.

Consistency links the named intervention to the potential outcome. No interference means one store’s assignment does not change another store’s outcome. Together with a well-defined treatment, these are often discussed under SUTVA. If stores share inventory or staff, design the assignment level to match those connections.

Controlled and natural experiments differ in who assigns

Find the source of the comparison
DesignSource of variation
Controlled experimentThe research or operating team assigns the alternative policies.
Natural experimentAn external rule or event creates plausibly comparable exposure.

An external change is useful only when its assignment story supports the counterfactual comparison. A policy change alone does not guarantee comparability. The retail pilot uses explicit random offers; the later rollout has a different assignment process and will require a different analysis.

Compare the randomized groups

Pilot outcomes in weeks 17–24
AssignmentStoresMean stockout rate (%)Mean weekly cost (CU)
Usual operations2511.94100.26
Alert offer258.4590.98

Estimated reduction = 11.94% − 8.45% = 3.49 percentage points

Random assignment creates the basis for the comparison before outcomes are measured. The difference in average post-period rates estimates the effect of the alert offer for this pilot population. A positive reduction means fewer stockout product-days under the alert policy.

The 95% interval for the reduction runs from 2.36 to 4.62 percentage points. It uses variation across the 25 store averages in each group. The appendix shows the independent-groups standard error and t multiplier.

Follow this calculation further →

Translate the service result into the cost decision

One percentage point corresponds to 1.4 product-days out of the fixed weekly exposure of 140. At 6 CU each, that is 8.40 CU in accounting cost. Divide the 20 CU weekly alert cost by 8.40 to find the break-even improvement.

Break-even reduction = 20 ÷ (140 × 0.01 × 6) = 2.38 percentage points

Estimated weekly saving = 8.40 × 3.49 − 20 = 9.28 CU per store

The estimated saving is positive, with a 95% interval from -0.22 to 18.78 CU. The service improvement is clear in this pilot, while the cost estimate is close enough to break-even at its lower endpoint to make staged expansion useful.

This is where the precision introduced in Lesson 3 becomes part of a spending decision. Reporting only the mean reduction would omit the cost threshold; reporting only whether a statistical test rejects zero would omit whether the gain pays for the service.

Connect the effect to a rollout rule

An A/B comparison can also be written as regression

Store outcome = intercept + offer coefficient × D + residual

With only an intercept and a binary offer, the fitted coefficient equals offered mean minus usual-operation mean. Its negative is our reported stockout reduction. Analyze the store-level follow-up means because assignment took place at the store level, even though each store supplies many product-days.

Use primary outcomes and guardrails together

  • Primary outcome: reduction in stockout rate.
  • Financial translation: stockout charge avoided minus alert cost.
  • Implementation records: delivery of alerts and staff review effort.
  • Guardrails: inventory and service problems elsewhere.

The case includes stockout counts and an explicit accounting cost rule. Staff effort and other operating guardrails are requirements for the next real implementation, not additional observed results in this dataset. Pre-specify the review horizon and replicate important findings in the next phase.

Use the known answer to check the reasoning

After making the pilot decision: reveal both paths

Across the pilot’s realized potential outcomes: ATE = 3.72, ATT = 3.61, ATU = 3.83 points.

The observed group reduction equals ATT plus a selection component of -0.12 points in this particular randomized draw. That finite-sample difference can occur by chance; the randomization argument concerns the assignment process across repetitions.

The generated world lets us compare the actual assignment-based estimate with normally unobserved targets. Use this reveal to check the estimator after making the decision from the factual data.

Choose the next learning investment

Recommend a measured next phase rather than treating the pilot average as the return at every store. Record service delivery, staff workload, and the extra inventory associated with the alerts. The same cost rule should follow the policy into the next phase so that apparent savings do not come from changing the accounting definition.

The director also has evidence from a separate group of stores that adopted voluntarily. Those stores were not randomized, but their operating histories may tell us about a different rollout population. The next lesson reconstructs their selection process before estimating a policy effect.

Update the decision memo

Pilot offer reduces stockouts by 3.49 points (95% interval 2.36–4.62). Under the stated cost rule, estimated saving is 9.28 CU/store-week, with interval -0.22–18.78. Fund a measured next phase with the same service and cost definitions.

Make the call

Why is the break-even threshold above zero even if every reduction in stockouts is desirable?

Compare your reasoning

The policy costs 20 CU per store-week. The accounting benefit has to cover that cost before the policy saves money. The threshold is 20 divided by the saving associated with one percentage point.

The bigger picture

An intervention decision asks what changes because the business acts. A randomized offer gives that question a concrete comparison; the cost threshold translates it into a spending choice. Forecasting and evaluation therefore contribute different pieces to the same operational plan.

After your decision: open the known answer

The expected alert reduction across all 50 pilot stores is 3.81 percentage points in the shared world. The estimated group contrast differs because assignment and observed stockout counts vary in this realization.
